title: CSF and Synovial Fluid: Meningitis, Bleeding Taps and Hot Joints
summary: Interpret CSF in bacterial meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage (three-tube test, xanthochromia timing), read gout and pseudogout crystals, and avoid the classic synovial traps in septic arthritis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 30 Hits 1, 5, 6 and 7 and Traps 1 and 4. Checked against Tumani 2020 (German S1 CSF guideline), Hrishi 2019, Doherty & Forbes 2014, Huy 2010, Long 2019 and Ragab 2017. Hit 5 characterizes septic arthritis by WBC 50,000–200,000 with low glucose; Long 2019 notes overlap with crystal arthritis, ~half of septic joints ≤ 28,000/µL, and no useful change from synovial glucose (register flag rv-septic-synovial). Not taught: CSF glucose < 40 mg/dL and ratio < 0.3, lactate > 35 mg/dL as a single cut-off, xanthochromia peaking at days 2–4 and lasting 2–4 weeks, and the traumatic-tap correction (1 WBC per 700 RBCs) — not in the sources read.

objectives: State normal CSF values and interpret CSF in bacterial meningitis.
Distinguish a traumatic tap from subarachnoid hemorrhage and know the timing limit of xanthochromia.
Identify MSU and CPPD crystals by shape and birefringence.
Interpret synovial fluid in suspected septic arthritis without over-relying on cell counts, glucose or crystals.

scenes.title: Bloody CSF and a crystal-filled knee
scenes.altText: Three cards. Card A: thunderclap headache 8 hours ago, CT normal; LP tubes 1→3 all pink. Card B: fever and neck stiffness; CSF cloudy, neutrophils high, glucose ratio 0.2. Card C: hot swollen knee in a man with gout; synovial WBC 38,000/µL, needle-shaped crystals seen. A question token: “Bleed or tap? Bacterial or not? Crystals — case closed?” The cartoon scientist holds three tubes.

cues.text: Patient A had a thunderclap headache eight hours ago. CT is normal, and all three spinal-fluid tubes look pink.
Patient B has fever and a stiff neck. The CSF is cloudy, full of neutrophils, with a glucose ratio of 0.2.
Patient C, a man with gout, has a hot swollen knee: 38,000 white cells and needle-shaped crystals. Is that case closed?

props.label: Bleed or tap? Bacterial? Crystals — closed?

scenes.title: Normal CSF and normal synovial fluid
scenes.altText: A reference card for CSF (German S1 guideline 2020): cells < 5/µL (lymphomonocytic); total protein < 500 mg/L; CSF/serum glucose ratio > 0.50; lactate 0.9–2.7 mmol/L (age-dependent). A note: always pair CSF glucose with a blood glucose. A synovial card: normal joint fluid is clear and viscous with few cells; synovial culture is the single most important test whenever fluid is aspirated. A polarized-light card: MSU (gout) crystals are needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent (yellow parallel to the compensator axis); CPPD (pseudogout) crystals are usually rhomboid, positively birefringent (blue).

cues.text: Normal CSF has fewer than 5 cells per microlitre, mostly lymphocytes and monocytes, and total protein below 500 milligrams per litre.
The CSF-to-serum glucose ratio is normally above 0.5, so always draw a blood glucose with the tap. CSF lactate is normally about 0.9 to 2.7 millimoles per litre.
In joint fluid, culture is the single most important test whenever fluid is aspirated.
Under polarized light, gout crystals, monosodium urate, are needles with strong negative birefringence: yellow when parallel to the compensator axis.
Pseudogout crystals, calcium pyrophosphate, are usually rhomboid with positive birefringence, appearing blue in the same orientation.

scenes.title: Bacterial meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage
scenes.altText: A bacterial meningitis card: neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low CSF/serum glucose ratio, raised lactate. CSF lactate meta-analysis (Huy 2010): pooled sensitivity ~0.96; published cut-offs range 2.1–4.44 mmol/L, so each centre sets its own; prior antibiotics lower it. An SAH card: three-tube test — RBCs that fall from tube 1 to tube 3 suggest a traumatic tap; evenly bloody tubes plus xanthochromia point to SAH. Xanthochromia (pigment from lysed RBCs: oxyhemoglobin, then bilirubin) is detected best by spectrophotometry; it and erythrophagocytosis may be absent < 12 hours after the bleed. Protect the xanthochromia sample from light.

cues.text: Bacterial meningitis gives a neutrophil-rich pleocytosis, high protein, a low CSF-to-serum glucose ratio and a raised lactate.
In a meta-analysis, CSF lactate was about 96 percent sensitive, but published cut-offs ranged from 2.1 to 4.4 millimoles per litre, so each laboratory sets its own.
For subarachnoid hemorrhage, collect three tubes. Red cells that fall from tube one to tube three suggest a traumatic tap; evenly bloody tubes favour a bleed.
Xanthochromia, the yellow pigment from lysed red cells, oxyhemoglobin and then bilirubin, is best detected by spectrophotometry. Protect that sample from light.
But xanthochromia and red-cell-eating macrophages may be absent less than 12 hours after the bleed, so an early tap can look like a traumatic one.

scenes.title: Septic arthritis: counts overlap, crystals don’t exclude
scenes.altText: A synovial card (Long 2019 review): a synovial WBC ≥ 50,000/µL raises the likelihood of septic arthritis but also occurs in gout and pseudogout; nearly half of culture-proven septic joints have ≤ 28,000/µL; > 90% neutrophils increases likelihood; Gram stain sensitivity ~29–65% for gram-positive infection (lower for gram-negative, ~25% gonococcal); synovial protein and glucose do not meaningfully change the likelihood; crystals do NOT rule out septic arthritis; culture grows in ~80% of nongonococcal cases. Back to the hook: A — early SAH (evenly bloody, < 12 h: repeat/spectrophotometry); B — bacterial meningitis; C — culture the joint despite crystals.

cues.text: A synovial count of 50,000 or more raises the chance of septic arthritis, but gout and pseudogout can reach it too, and nearly half of culture-proven septic joints have 28,000 or fewer.
More than 90 percent neutrophils increases the likelihood. The Gram stain misses many infections: sensitivity about 29 to 65 percent for gram-positives, and less for gram-negatives and gonococci.
Synovial protein and glucose do not meaningfully change the probability.
And crystals do not rule out infection; gout and a septic joint can coexist. Culture grows the organism in about 80 percent of nongonococcal cases.
So A may be an early subarachnoid bleed, B is bacterial meningitis, and C needs a joint culture despite the crystals.

props.title: Synovial fluid in a hot joint

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Bloody first tube = SAH” (✓ compare tubes 1–3 and look for xanthochromia; very early SAH may lack it); “Crystals in the joint — no antibiotics needed” (✓ crystals don’t exclude infection; culture); “Synovial WBC 30,000 rules out septic arthritis” (✓ nearly half of septic joints have ≤ 28,000).

cues.text: Trap one: a bloody first tube means subarachnoid hemorrhage. Compare tubes one to three, and look for xanthochromia, remembering it may be absent very early.
Trap two: crystals in the joint mean no antibiotics are needed. Crystals do not exclude infection. Send a culture.
Trap three: a synovial count of 30,000 rules out septic arthritis. Nearly half of septic joints have counts of 28,000 or fewer.

scenes.title: Gout points negative; the tubes tell time
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Needles are negative (MSU), rhomboids are positive (CPPD); the three tubes tell you where the blood came from, and yellow tells you how long it has been there.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: needles are negative, rhomboids are positive. The three tubes tell you where the blood came from, and yellow tells you how long it has been there.
Where it breaks: crystal shapes vary and polarizing technique matters; xanthochromia may be absent early; and no single synovial count separates infection from crystal arthritis.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “CSF: glucose ratio > 0.5 normal · bacterial: PMN ↑, protein ↑, ratio ↓, lactate ↑ · SAH: even tubes + xanthochromia (may lag < 12 h)”, “Synovial: always culture · crystals don’t exclude infection · MSU needles strong −, CPPD rhomboids +”.

cues.text: Pair CSF glucose with blood glucose, use tubes and xanthochromia for bleeding, and in a hot joint culture the fluid even when crystals are present.

props.label: CSF: ratio > 0.5 normal · bacterial: PMN, protein ↑, ratio ↓, lactate ↑ · SAH: even tubes + yellow
Synovial: always culture · crystals ≠ no infection · MSU strong −, CPPD +

explanation.what: Plain language: spinal fluid and joint fluid tell you whether there is infection, bleeding or crystals, but each test has blind spots. Scientific terms: pleocytosis, CSF/serum glucose ratio, CSF lactate, three-tube test, xanthochromia, erythrophagocytosis, monosodium urate (MSU), calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD), birefringence, red compensator.
explanation.why: Bacteria and neutrophils consume glucose and produce lactate; inflammation raises protein. Blood in the subarachnoid space lyses over hours, releasing oxyhemoglobin and then bilirubin (xanthochromia); a traumatic tap adds blood mainly to the first tubes. MSU and CPPD crystals differ in shape and optical sign.
explanation.measure: Normal CSF: cells < 5/µL, protein < 500 mg/L, glucose ratio > 0.50, lactate 0.9–2.7 mmol/L. CSF lactate cut-offs in studies 2.1–4.44 mmol/L (pooled sensitivity ~0.96). Xanthochromia by spectrophotometry; may be absent < 12 h. Synovial: ≥ 50,000/µL not specific; ~half of septic joints ≤ 28,000/µL; > 90% PMN increases likelihood; Gram stain 29–65% sensitive (gram-positive); culture positive in ~80% of nongonococcal cases.
explanation.differs: Bacterial (PMN, low glucose ratio, high lactate) vs aseptic meningitis. Traumatic tap (RBC falling tube 1→3, no xanthochromia) vs SAH (even RBCs, xanthochromia after ~12 h). MSU (needles, strong negative) vs CPPD (rhomboid, positive).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: CSF patterns in meningitis, three-tube test and xanthochromia, crystal birefringence, and “crystals don’t exclude infection.”

comparisons.title: MSU vs CPPD crystals
comparisons.distinguisher: Shape and optical sign under compensated polarized light.

mnemonic.text: Needles are negative, rhomboids are positive; the tubes tell where, the yellow tells when.
mnemonic.explanation: MSU needles are strongly negatively birefringent and CPPD rhomboids positive; the three-tube trend localizes blood and xanthochromia dates it.
mnemonic.limitation: Crystal shapes vary and technique matters; xanthochromia may be absent early; no synovial count separates infection from crystal arthritis.

takeaway: Pair CSF glucose with blood glucose, use tubes and xanthochromia for bleeding, and in a hot joint culture the fluid even when crystals are present.

questions.stem: CSF tubes 1 to 3 have RBC counts of 12,000, 4,000 and 300/µL, with a clear colourless supernatant 18 hours after headache onset. What is the best interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Falling RBCs across tubes and no xanthochromia well after 12 hours favour a traumatic tap.
Incorrect. SAH gives evenly bloody tubes and, after ~12 hours, xanthochromia.
Incorrect. The CSF pattern itself is informative.

questions.stem: Synovial fluid from a hot knee shows needle-shaped crystals that are yellow when parallel to the compensator axis, and 42,000 WBC/µL with 92% neutrophils. What should be done?

options.text: Report MSU crystals and send synovial culture — crystals do not exclude infection
options.rationale: Correct. Gout and septic arthritis can coexist; culture is the most important test.
Incorrect. Crystals do not rule out septic arthritis.
Incorrect. CPPD crystals are usually rhomboid and positively birefringent (blue when parallel).

options.text: Exclude infection because WBC is below 50,000
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many septic joints have counts below 50,000.

questions.stem: Why should a blood glucose be drawn at the time of lumbar puncture?

options.text: CSF glucose is interpreted as a CSF/serum ratio (normally > 0.5)
options.rationale: Correct. The ratio corrects for the patient’s blood glucose.

options.text: To check for hypoglycemia caused by the procedure
options.rationale: Incorrect. The purpose is interpreting CSF glucose.

options.text: Blood glucose is needed to calculate CSF lactate

options.rationale: Incorrect. Without blood glucose, a CSF glucose can be misread.

claims.text: Normal CSF values; bacterial meningitis pattern; lactate cut-offs vary 2.1–4.44 mmol/L, pooled sensitivity ~0.96; pair blood glucose.
Three-tube test; xanthochromia by spectrophotometry, light-protected; may be absent < 12 h.
MSU needles strongly negative (yellow ∥); CPPD rhomboid positive (blue ∥).
Synovial counts overlap; ~half septic ≤ 28,000; PMN > 90%; Gram 29–65%; protein/glucose unhelpful; crystals don’t exclude; culture most important.
CSF glucose < 40 mg/dL and ratio < 0.3; lactate > 35 mg/dL; xanthochromia peaks days 2–4 and lasts 2–4 weeks; traumatic tap correction 1 WBC per 700 RBCs and 8 mg/dL protein per 10,000 RBCs.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 5 defines septic arthritis by synovial WBC 50,000–200,000/µL with > 90% PMNs and low glucose; Long 2019 notes such counts also occur in gout and pseudogout, nearly half of culture-proven septic joints have ≤ 28,000/µL, and synovial glucose does not meaningfully change the likelihood. The lesson teaches the overlap.
